title: Finasteride and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Propecia?
excerpt: Can you drink on finasteride? There's no known direct interaction, but alcohol and finasteride share side effects on libido, erections, and mood. Here's what matters for hair loss and prostate use.
metaDescription: Can you drink on finasteride? There's no known direct interaction, but both affect libido and mood. What to know for Propecia and Proscar.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no known direct interaction between finasteride and alcohol. Finasteride (sold as Propecia for hair loss and Proscar for an enlarged prostate) is not affected by alcohol in any way that changes how well it works, and its official prescribing information carries no alcohol warning. For most healthy men, a few drinks while on finasteride is considered fine. The real overlap is in side effects: both alcohol and finasteride can lower sex drive, make erections less reliable, and affect mood. That overlap, plus a few situations involving the liver, the prostate, and other medicines, is what this page covers.

**The quick rules:** Keep taking finasteride on your normal daily schedule; you don't need to skip a dose because you're drinking. Keep drinking moderate, since heavy drinking can mimic or worsen the side effects people worry about with finasteride. If you notice low libido, erection problems, or a low mood, try a stretch of alcohol-free days before blaming the pill, and tell your doctor about anything that lasts. If you have liver disease or take other prescriptions, check with your doctor or pharmacist.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor if** you have liver disease or abnormal liver tests, you drink heavily on most days, you take other prescription medicines (especially for blood pressure, the prostate, or mood), or you notice changes in sex drive, erections, ejaculation, breast tenderness or lumps, or mood while on finasteride. **Get help right away** if you have thoughts of harming yourself: in the US, call or text 988, or call 911 in an emergency.

## How Finasteride Works, and Why Alcohol Doesn't Block It

Finasteride belongs to a group of drugs called 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors. That's a mouthful, but the idea is simple. Your body uses an enzyme called 5-alpha-reductase to turn testosterone into a stronger hormone called **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)**. DHT is the hormone that shrinks hair follicles on the scalp in male-pattern hair loss, and it's also the hormone that drives prostate growth as men age.

Finasteride blocks one form of that enzyme (type II), so less testosterone gets converted into DHT. At the 1 mg dose used for hair loss, blood DHT levels drop substantially, by around two-thirds in the clinical trials. At the 5 mg dose used for the prostate, the effect is similar, and over months the prostate gradually shrinks.

Here's why alcohol doesn't get in the way:

- **Different targets.** Finasteride works by binding to 5-alpha-reductase. Alcohol doesn't bind to that enzyme or stop finasteride from doing so.
- **Different clean-up routes.** Finasteride is broken down in the liver, mainly by an enzyme called **CYP3A4**. Alcohol is mostly broken down by a different set of enzymes (alcohol dehydrogenase and, in heavier drinkers, CYP2E1). They don't compete for the same main pathway in any way known to matter.
- **The effect outlasts the pill.** Finasteride itself clears the blood within a day or so, but its effect on the enzyme lasts much longer. Even if a heavy night somehow changed how one dose was handled, the drop in DHT is maintained by steady daily use, not by any single dose.

That's why you won't find alcohol listed among finasteride's drug interactions in its US prescribing information. In fact, the label lists no clinically important drug interactions at all, which is unusual for a daily medicine.

## What the Research and Official Guidance Actually Say

Most of what's known here comes from the drug's prescribing information and its large clinical trials, plus what's known about alcohol's own effects on the body.

**No direct interaction has been identified.** Finasteride has been prescribed since the early 1990s for the prostate and since the late 1990s for hair loss. In that time no meaningful alcohol interaction has been established, and the labels for both Propecia and Proscar don't tell patients to avoid alcohol.

**There are no trials of finasteride plus alcohol.** It's worth being honest about this. Nobody has run a study giving men finasteride and then a set amount of alcohol to look for problems. The reassurance comes from how the drug works, how it's cleared, and decades of use by men who drink, not from a trial designed to answer this exact question.

**The side effects are the real story.** The prescribing information lists sexual side effects (lower libido, erection problems, and changes in ejaculation) in a small minority of men in clinical trials, slightly more often than with a placebo. Breast tenderness or enlargement is also listed. After the drug was on the market, the FDA added warnings that some men report sexual side effects continuing after they stop the drug, and later added depression and thoughts of self-harm to the list of reported side effects. Whether finasteride causes these lasting problems, sometimes called post-finasteride syndrome, is still debated among researchers, but the reports are taken seriously enough to be on the label.

**Alcohol has well-documented effects in the same areas.** Alcohol is a depressant that, in larger amounts, reduces erectile function, dulls sexual response, and can worsen low mood and anxiety over the following day. Long-term heavy drinking is linked to lower testosterone and to sexual problems on its own. So even without any chemical interaction, the two can pile up on the same parts of your life.

## The Real Overlap: Libido, Erections, and Mood

This is the part that matters most for men who drink socially and take finasteride.

### Sexual side effects

If you've noticed that things aren't working as they used to, it's tempting to blame the pill, and sometimes that's right. But alcohol is a very common cause of the same problems:

- **A few drinks can blunt erections on the night.** Alcohol slows the nervous system and can make it harder to get and keep an erection, especially after several drinks. This is temporary and fades as the alcohol clears.
- **Regular heavy drinking can lower desire over time.** Long-term heavy drinking is linked to lower testosterone and reduced sex drive. Our guide to [alcohol and testosterone](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-testosterone) explains how that works, and [alcohol and libido](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-libido) covers the short-term effects.
- **Finasteride's own effect is usually steady.** If finasteride is causing a sexual side effect, it tends to show up whether or not you've been drinking.

A practical test: if problems only appear on nights you drink, alcohol is the likely cause. If they're there on sober days too, especially if they started after you began finasteride, that's worth a conversation with your doctor. Don't stop or change a prescription on your own without talking it through, but don't sit on it either.

If you use an erection medicine such as sildenafil or tadalafil, alcohol has its own interaction with those (mainly dizziness and low blood pressure). See our pages on [Viagra and alcohol](/never-hungover/viagra-and-alcohol) and [Cialis and alcohol](/never-hungover/cialis-and-alcohol).

### Mood

Alcohol can leave people feeling flat, anxious, or low the next day, something often called "hangxiety." Finasteride's label lists depression among the side effects reported after it went on the market. Neither of these means you'll have a problem, but if you already notice low moods on finasteride, drinking can make those days worse.

**Pay attention if your mood drops and stays down**, whether or not you've been drinking. Tell your doctor about persistent low mood, loss of interest in things, or anxiety that doesn't lift. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, get help right away: in the US, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline), or call 911 in an emergency.

## Does Alcohol Undo Finasteride's Effect on Hair Loss?

This is one of the most searched questions, and the short answer is no. There is no good evidence that drinking reduces finasteride's ability to lower DHT or slows its effect on hair.

You'll find claims online that alcohol "raises DHT" or "cancels out" finasteride. These don't hold up well. Alcohol's best-documented hormonal effects run in the other direction: heavy drinking tends to lower testosterone, not raise DHT. Even if alcohol nudged hormone levels slightly, finasteride would still be blocking the enzyme that makes DHT.

That said, drinking isn't neutral for hair in general. Heavy drinking can affect hair indirectly through:

- **Poor sleep**, which alcohol reliably disrupts in the second half of the night
- **Low intake of nutrients** such as protein, iron, and zinc when drinking replaces meals
- **Stress and dehydration**, which affect skin and scalp health

None of these are reasons to panic over a few drinks at the weekend. They're reasons not to expect hair results from finasteride while drinking heavily most nights. For more on this, see our guide to [whether alcohol causes hair loss](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-hair-loss).

### What about topical finasteride and minoxidil solutions?

Many topical hair-loss products, including liquid minoxidil and some compounded topical finasteride sprays, are made with alcohol as a solvent. That alcohol sits on your scalp and is not a drinking concern; very little gets into your blood. It can, however, dry or irritate the scalp, which is why some people switch to foam versions without the solvent. If irritation is a problem, ask your doctor or pharmacist about alternatives. Note that the FDA has issued a warning about compounded topical finasteride products, so it's worth getting these through a doctor who can explain the risks.

## Finasteride, Alcohol, and the Liver

Finasteride is processed in the liver, so it's fair to ask whether drinking adds risk.

For healthy men, there's no evidence that moderate drinking and finasteride together harm the liver. Liver injury from finasteride is rare. The prescribing information advises caution in people with reduced liver function, because the liver is the main route for clearing the drug and a struggling liver can let levels build up.

That makes a difference if you:

- Drink heavily on most days
- Have fatty liver disease, hepatitis, or cirrhosis
- Have been told your liver enzymes are high

In those cases, the issue isn't really a finasteride-alcohol interaction. It's that the liver needs attention, and your doctor should know about both your drinking and the medicine. If you're curious about how your liver handles alcohol in general, our overview of [alcohol and medications](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) covers the bigger picture of how common drugs and drinking share the liver.

## Proscar, Prostate Symptoms, and Drinking

Men taking finasteride at the 5 mg dose (Proscar) for an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH, have a separate set of practical concerns.

### Alcohol can worsen urinary symptoms

Proscar is meant to reduce urinary symptoms such as weak flow, frequent urination, and getting up at night. Alcohol works against that in a few ways:

- **It makes you produce more urine.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you need to pee more often. Our guide on [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee) explains this.
- **It can irritate the bladder**, adding to urgency.
- **Drinking late in the evening means more trips at night**, which is often the most bothersome BPH symptom.

The practical fix is simple: drink smaller amounts, drink earlier in the evening, and stop a few hours before bed.

A rare but serious problem to know about: in men with an enlarged prostate, a large amount of alcohol, sometimes combined with cold medicines containing decongestants or sedating antihistamines, can bring on **acute urinary retention**, where you suddenly can't pee at all. If that happens, it's a reason to go to urgent care or an emergency room, not to wait it out.

### Watch for combination prostate medicines

Finasteride is often prescribed alongside an alpha-blocker such as **tamsulosin (Flomax)**, doxazosin, or alfuzosin, which relaxes the prostate and bladder neck. These drugs can cause dizziness or light-headedness when you stand up, and alcohol can add to that. If you take a combination, stand up slowly after drinking and be careful at night when you get up to use the bathroom.

### Finasteride lowers PSA test results

This isn't about alcohol, but it's important enough to mention. Finasteride lowers PSA, the blood marker used to screen for prostate cancer, by roughly half after several months. If you're having PSA tests, make sure the doctor reading them knows you take finasteride, so the result is interpreted correctly.

## Who Should Be More Careful

You don't need to avoid alcohol entirely on finasteride, but more caution makes sense if you:

- **Drink heavily or binge regularly.** The side-effect overlap is bigger, and liver concerns come into play.
- **Have liver disease** or abnormal liver tests.
- **Take an alpha-blocker** for the prostate, or blood pressure medicines that can cause dizziness.
- **Already have sexual side effects or low mood** on finasteride.
- **Have an enlarged prostate with significant urinary symptoms**, or have had urinary retention before.

And a safety note that applies regardless of drinking: women who are or may become pregnant should not handle crushed or broken finasteride tablets, because the drug can be absorbed through the skin and can affect the development of a male baby. Keep the tablets whole and stored safely.

## Practical Tips for Drinking on Finasteride

- **Keep your dosing routine.** Take finasteride at the same time each day. There's no need to skip it before or after drinking.
- **Don't double up after a missed dose.** If you forget one because of a late night, take the next one at your usual time.
- **Keep it moderate.** US dietary guidelines define moderate drinking as up to two drinks a day for men. Staying around that keeps alcohol's own sexual and mood effects in check.
- **Separate the two causes.** If something feels off, a couple of alcohol-free weeks is an easy way to see what's driving it.
- **Eat and hydrate.** Drinking with food and alternating with water helps your sleep, your mood the next day, and, if you have prostate symptoms, your nights.
- **Tell your doctor the truth about how much you drink.** It helps them interpret side effects and liver tests.

## A Note on Hangover Supplements

If you're reading this because you want to keep enjoying a night out while protecting your hair and health, the biggest wins are the basic ones: drink less, drink slower, eat beforehand, and alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There are no studies on DHM taken with finasteride, and no known reason they would clash, but "no known reason" isn't the same as tested. Check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding it to any prescription. If you do decide to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

No supplement changes how you should use finasteride. Take it as prescribed, and raise side effects with your doctor rather than trying to offset them with something else.

## The Bottom Line

- There is no known direct interaction between finasteride and alcohol, and the label has no alcohol warning.
- Alcohol does not block finasteride or cancel its effect on DHT or hair loss.
- The real overlap is in side effects: both can lower libido, affect erections, and worsen mood. Heavy drinking makes that overlap bigger.
- With Proscar for the prostate, alcohol can worsen urinary symptoms, and it adds to the dizziness from alpha-blockers like tamsulosin.
- If you have liver disease, take other prescriptions, or notice side effects that don't go away, talk to your doctor. If you have thoughts of self-harm, call or text 988 in the US right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I drink alcohol while taking finasteride?**

For most healthy men, yes. Finasteride (Propecia for hair loss, Proscar for an enlarged prostate) has no known direct interaction with alcohol, and its prescribing information does not include an alcohol warning. Moderate drinking is generally considered compatible with it. The overlap to watch is in side effects: both alcohol and finasteride can lower sex drive and affect erections and mood. If you have liver disease, take other medicines, or notice new side effects, talk to your doctor.

**Does alcohol make finasteride less effective for hair loss?**

There is no good evidence that alcohol stops finasteride from lowering DHT or slows its effect on hair. The drug works by blocking an enzyme, and alcohol does not block that action. Heavy drinking can still be hard on hair in other ways, through poor sleep, poor nutrition, and stress, so a pattern of heavy drinking may work against the overall goal even if it does not cancel the pill.

**How long after drinking can I take finasteride?**

There is no required waiting period. Finasteride does not need to be timed around drinks, and you can take your usual daily dose on its normal schedule, including the morning after a night out. If you are being sick, take it once you can keep it down rather than doubling up later. A missed dose is not dangerous; just take the next one at the usual time.

**Does finasteride affect the liver, and does alcohol add to that?**

Finasteride is broken down in the liver, mainly by an enzyme called CYP3A4, while alcohol is mostly handled by other enzymes. Serious liver problems from finasteride are rare, but the label advises caution in people with reduced liver function because the drug can build up. If you drink heavily on a regular basis or have fatty liver, hepatitis, or abnormal liver tests, your doctor should know before you start or continue finasteride.

**Can alcohol make finasteride sexual side effects worse?**

It can add to them. Finasteride causes lower libido, erection problems, or changes in ejaculation in a small minority of men. Alcohol, especially several drinks in one sitting, also makes erections harder to get and keep. The two are not known to interact chemically, but their effects can stack. If you notice problems, try a few alcohol-free nights first to see which is responsible, and raise any lasting change with your doctor.

**Is it safe to drink on Proscar with an enlarged prostate?**

Proscar itself has no direct alcohol interaction. The practical issue is urination: alcohol makes you produce more urine and can irritate the bladder, which can worsen frequency, urgency, and getting up at night, the exact symptoms Proscar is meant to ease. Many men with an enlarged prostate also take tamsulosin (Flomax) or a similar drug, and alcohol can add to its dizziness when standing. Drinking earlier in the evening and in smaller amounts tends to help.

**Does alcohol affect dutasteride the same way?**

Dutasteride (Avodart) works in a similar way to finasteride and also has no known direct interaction with alcohol. The same side-effect overlaps apply: libido, erections, and mood. Dutasteride stays in the body much longer than finasteride, so side effects can take longer to fade after stopping. The same advice applies: moderate drinking is generally fine, and your doctor should hear about any new symptoms.

**Can DHM be taken with finasteride?**

There are no published studies on DHM and finasteride together, and no known reason they would clash, but there is also no data showing it is safe. DHM is a plant compound studied mainly in animals for its effects on alcohol metabolism. If you want to try it while taking finasteride or any other prescription, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
